We begin by developing a rigorous definition of irreducible multi-dimensional features based on whether they can be decomposed into either independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features. Motivated by these definitions, we design a scalable method that uses sparse autoencoders to automatically find multi-dimensional features in GPT-2 and Mistral 7B. These auto-discovered features include strikingly interpretable examples, e.g. circular features representing days of the week and months of the year. We identify tasks where these exact circles are used to solve computational problems involving modular arithmetic in days of the week and months of the year. Next, we provide evidence that these circular features are indeed the fundamental unit of computation in these tasks with intervention experiments on Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B, and we examine the continuity of the days of the week feature in Mistral 7B. Overall, our work argues that understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary to mechanistically decompose some model behaviors.

papers.title: Reasoning or Retrieval? A Study of Answer Attribution on Large Reasoning Models
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) exhibit unprecedented capabilities in solving complex problems through Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning. However, recent studies reveal that their final answers often contradict their own reasoning traces. We hypothesize that this inconsistency stems from two competing mechanisms for generating answers: CoT reasoning and memory retrieval. To test this hypothesis, we conduct controlled experiments that challenge LRMs with misleading cues during reasoning and/or corrupted answers during retrieval. Our results across models and datasets confirm that both mechanisms operate simultaneously, with their relative dominance influenced by multiple factors: problem domains, model scales, and fine-tuning approaches (e.g., reinforcement learning vs. distillation). The findings reveal a critical limitation in current reasoning fine-tuning paradigms: models can exploit the retrieval mechanism as a shortcut, effectively "hacking" the reward signal and undermining genuine reasoning development. To address this challenge, we introduce FARL, a novel fine-tuning framework that integrates memory unlearning with reinforcement learning. By carefully suppressing retrieval shortcuts during the fine-tuning process, FARL promotes reasoning-dominant behavior and enhances generalizable reasoning capabilities.

papers.title: How Much Does Attention Actually Attend? Questioning the Importance of Attention in Pretrained Transformers
papers.research_question: How much do pretrained Transformers rely on the input-dependent attention mechanism?
papers.core_contribution: Pretrained language models can achieve competitive performance even when their input-dependent attention matrices are replaced with constant matrices, suggesting the attention mechanism is not as crucial as previously believed.
papers.conclusion: Attention in pretrained Transformers is not as important as typically thought, motivating research on simpler alternatives and better utilization of the attention mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
Replacing all input-dependent attention matrices with constant ones leads to an average relative performance drop of only 8%.
Half of the attention matrices can be replaced with constant ones without loss in performance, and sometimes performance even improves.
Better-performing models suffer more when attention is removed, indicating they rely more on the input-dependent attention mechanism.
The constant matrices generated by PAPA often exhibit diagonal patterns and focus on special tokens like [CLS] and [SEP].
The method is not very sensitive to the dataset used for generating the constant matrices.
papers.limitation:
PAPA is based on probing rather than fine-tuning, so attention in fine-tuned models might behave differently.
The constant matrices are constructed by averaging, which might not be optimal; better construction methods could further reduce the gap.
The analysis is limited to six English tasks, and results might differ for other tasks and languages.
future_direction: Developing novel Transformer architectures with more efficient attention mechanisms.
Improving the utilization of the attention mechanism in Transformer variants.
Exploring knowledge distillation of existing PLMs into attention-free models.
papers.abstract: The attention mechanism is considered the backbone of the widely-used Transformer architecture. It contextualizes the input by computing input-specific attention matrices. We find that this mechanism, while powerful and elegant, is not as important as typically thought for pretrained language models. We introduce PAPA, a new probing method that replaces the input-dependent attention matrices with constant ones—the average attention weights over multiple inputs. We use PAPA to analyze several established pretrained Transformers on six downstream tasks. We find that without any input-dependent attention, all models achieve competitive performance—an average relative drop of only 8% from the probing baseline. Further, little or no performance drop is observed when replacing half of the input-dependent attention matrices with constant (input-independent) ones. Interestingly, we show that better-performing models lose more from applying our method than weaker models, suggesting that the utilization of the input-dependent attention mechanism might be a factor in their success. Our results motivate research on simpler alternatives to input-dependent attention, as well as on methods for better utilization of this mechanism in the Transformer architecture.

papers.title: When More is Less: Understanding Chain-of-Thought Length in LLMs
papers.research_question: Does reasoning performance consistently improve as Chain-of-Thought (CoT) processes grow longer, and what is the optimal CoT length?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that an optimal Chain-of-Thought length exists, following an inverted U-shaped curve with performance, and that this optimal length scales with task difficulty and model capability, revealing a simplicity bias where more capable models prefer shorter CoTs.
papers.conclusion: CoT length should be calibrated adaptively based on task complexity and model capability to optimize reasoning performance, moving beyond the assumption that longer is always better.
papers.key_findings:
Task accuracy versus CoT length follows an inverted U-shaped curve, indicating an optimal length.
The optimal CoT length increases with task difficulty but decreases with model capability (simplicity bias).
Reinforcement learning training guides models towards generating CoTs of optimal length.
Training models on data with optimal-length CoTs improves their reasoning performance.
Filtering out excessively long CoTs at inference using a length-aware voting method improves accuracy.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) employ Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning to deconstruct complex problems. While longer CoTs are often presumed superior, this paper challenges that notion, arguing that longer is not always better. Drawing on combined evidence from real-world observations, controlled experiments, and theoretical analysis, we demonstrate that task accuracy typically follows an inverted U-shaped curve with CoT length, where performance initially improves but eventually decreases as the number of CoT steps increases. With controlled experiments, we further uncover the scaling behaviors of the optimal CoT length: it increases with task difficulty but decreases with model capability, exposing an inherent simplicity bias where more capable models favor shorter, more efficient CoT reasoning. This bias is also evident in Reinforcement Learning (RL) training, where models gravitate towards shorter CoTs as their accuracy improves. To have a deep understanding of these dynamics, we establish a simple theoretical model that formally proves these phenomena, including the optimal length's scaling laws and the emergence of simplicity bias during RL. Guided by this framework, we demonstrate significant practical benefits from training with optimally-lengthed CoTs and employing length-aware filtering at inference. These findings offer both a principled understanding of the "overthinking" phenomenon and multiple practical guidelines for CoT calibration, enabling LLMs to achieve optimal reasoning performance with adaptive CoTs tailored to task complexity and model capability.

papers.title: AiR: Attention with Reasoning Capability
papers.research_question: How does attention progress to accomplish a task and is it reasonable? The paper investigates attention in the context of visual reasoning, proposing a framework to evaluate and improve attention based on reasoning processes.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the AiR framework, which includes a quantitative evaluation metric (AiR-E) for attention in reasoning, a supervision method (AiR-M) to progressively optimize attention, and an eye-tracking dataset (AiR-D).
papers.conclusion: The AiR framework effectively analyzes and models attention with improved reasoning capability and task performance.
papers.key_findings:
Humans who answer correctly have significantly higher attention accuracy (AiR-E) than those who answer incorrectly.
Humans consistently outperform machines in both attention accuracy and task performance.
Object-based attentions attend more accurately than spatial attentions.
Attention accuracy and task performance are correlated for humans, but for machines, spatial attention maps have low or negative correlations.
The proposed AiR-M supervision method improves attention accuracy and task performance over baselines and other supervision methods.
papers.abstract: While attention has been an increasingly popular component in deep neural networks to both interpret and boost performance of models, little work has examined how attention progresses to accomplish a task and whether it is reasonable. In this work, we propose an Attention with Reasoning capability (AiR) framework that uses attention to understand and improve the process leading to task outcomes. We first define an evaluation metric based on a sequence of atomic reasoning operations, enabling quantitative measurement of attention that considers the reasoning process. We then collect human eye-tracking and answer correctness data, and analyze various machine and human attentions on their reasoning capability and how they impact task performance. Furthermore, we propose a supervision method to jointly and progressively optimize attention, reasoning, and task performance so that models learn to look at regions of interests by following a reasoning process. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in analyzing and modeling attention with better reasoning capability and task performance. The code and data are available at https://github.com/szzexpoi/AiR

papers.title: Causal Head Gating: A Framework for Interpreting Roles of Attention Heads in Transformers
papers.research_question: How can we interpret the functional roles of attention heads in transformer models in a causal manner?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces causal head gating (CHG), a scalable method for causal interpretation of attention heads, and shows that LLMs contain multiple sparse task-sufficient sub-circuits, head roles are low modularity, and instruction following and in-context learning rely on separable mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: CHG is a flexible and scalable method for identifying causally relevant attention heads, revealing the distributed and context-dependent nature of computation in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
CHG scores yield causal insight validated via ablation and causal mediation analysis.
LLMs contain multiple sparse task-sufficient sub-circuits.
Individual head roles depend on interactions with others (low modularity).
Instruction following and in-context learning rely on separable mechanisms.
papers.limitation:
CHG does not reveal the precise computations performed by individual heads.
Occasional divergence between G+ and G- scores.
Head roles are context-dependent and vary across runs.
future_direction: Build on these tools to develop circuit-level explanations of how models implement complex behaviors.
papers.abstract: We present causal head gating (CHG), a scalable method for interpreting the functional roles of attention heads in transformer models. CHG learns soft gates over heads and assigns them a causal taxonomy - facilitating, interfering, or irrelevant - based on their impact on task performance. Unlike prior approaches in mechanistic interpretability, which are hypothesis-driven and require prompt templates or target labels, CHG applies directly to any dataset using standard next-token prediction. We evaluate CHG across multiple large language models (LLMs) in the Llama 3 model family and diverse tasks, including syntax, commonsense, and mathematical reasoning, and show that CHG scores yield causal, not merely correlational, insight validated via ablation and causal mediation analyses. We also introduce contrastive CHG, a variant that isolates sub-circuits for specific task components. Our findings reveal that LLMs contain multiple sparse task-sufficient sub-circuits, that individual head roles depend on interactions with others (low modularity), and that instruction following and in-context learning rely on separable mechanisms.

papers.title: Attention: Marginal Probability is All You Need?
papers.research_question: How can attention mechanisms be understood from a Bayesian probabilistic perspective, and how does this perspective unify different attentional architectures in machine learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a unifying Bayesian probabilistic framework for attention mechanisms, showing that transformer-style soft attention computes a marginal likelihood over possible network structures, and iterative attention mechanisms (e.g., slot attention) correspond to collapsed variational inference.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a Bayesian probabilistic framework that unifies diverse attention mechanisms in machine learning and neuroscience, offering a principled foundation for analysis and new architectural designs.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer attention (self-attention and cross-attention) can be viewed as computing an expectation over latent adjacency structures, where the softmax represents a posterior distribution over edges.
Iterative attention mechanisms, including slot-attention, block-slot-attention, and modern continuous Hopfield networks, can be derived as instances of collapsed variational inference within the same Bayesian framework.
The framework provides a bridge to Bayesian theories of attention in computational neuroscience, specifically by applying collapsed inference to Predictive Coding Networks.
The perspective clarifies the relationship between soft and hard attention, framing soft attention as exact marginalization and hard attention as a stochastic approximation, and suggests conditions under which hard attention is a good approximation.
The framework suggests new architectural designs can be created by altering the structural prior or potential functions of the underlying probabilistic model.
future_direction: Designing new attention mechanisms by altering the distribution that the mechanism marginalizes over, either by adjusting the structural prior or the potential functions.
papers.abstract: Attention mechanisms are a central property of cognitive systems allowing them to selectively deploy cognitive resources in a flexible manner. Attention has been long studied in the neurosciences and there are numerous phenomenological models that try to capture its core properties. Recently attentional mechanisms have become a dominating architectural choice of machine learning and are the central innovation of Transformers. The dominant intuition and formalism underlying their development has drawn on ideas of keys and queries in database management systems. In this work, we propose an alternative Bayesian foundation for attentional mechanisms and show how this unifies different attentional architectures in machine learning. This formulation allows to to identify commonality across different attention ML architectures as well as suggest a bridge to those developed in neuroscience. We hope this work will guide more sophisticated intuitions into the key properties of attention architectures and suggest new ones.

papers.title: Unveiling Reasoning Thresholds in Language Models: Scaling, Fine-Tuning, and Interpretability through Attention Maps
papers.research_question: What is the critical parameter threshold for reasoning abilities in decoder-only transformer-based language models, and how can fine-tuning and attention map analysis improve understanding of these capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies a critical parameter threshold (~1.6B) for reasoning abilities in language models, shows fine-tuning improves sub-threshold models, and uses attention maps to interpret reasoning processes.
papers.conclusion: The study identifies a critical parameter threshold for reasoning, demonstrates fine-tuning efficacy for sub-threshold models, and uses attention maps for interpretability, advancing understanding of reasoning in decoder-only transformer-based language models.
papers.key_findings:
Models above ~1.6 billion parameters show significant improvement in reasoning performance on tasks like commonsense QA and deductive reasoning.
Fine-tuning sub-threshold models with task-specific exemplars substantially improves performance on simpler deductive rules (e.g., implication elimination, conjunction introduction).
Attention map analysis reveals that models generating correct chain-of-thought exhibit higher token-level attention scores on subsequent correct tokens and correct parts of speech.
Parameter gaps exist for specific deductive rules: disjunction elimination (~1.1B) and proof by contradiction (~1.6B).
Smaller models (below threshold) struggle with structured answer formatting, resulting in high rates of unparseable responses.
papers.abstract: This study investigates the in-context learning capabilities of various decoder-only transformer-based language models with different model sizes and training data, including GPT2, SmolLM2, OpenELM, TinyLlama, Stable LM, and Gemma 2. We identify a critical parameter threshold (~1.6 billion), beyond which reasoning performance improves significantly in tasks such as commonsense reasoning in multiple-choice question answering and deductive reasoning. Specifically, models above this threshold achieve better success rates in chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting for deductive reasoning tasks, especially those requiring longer reasoning chains, such as proof by contradiction and disjunction elimination. To address limitations in sub-threshold models, we demonstrate that fine-tuning with task-specific exemplars substantially enhances reasoning performance, enabling accurate CoT generation even without additional exemplars in the prompt for tasks with shorter reasoning chains. Finally, our analysis of attention maps reveals that models capable of generating correct CoTs exhibit higher token-level attention scores on subsequent correct tokens and the correct parts of speech, providing interpretability insights into reasoning processes. These findings collectively advance understanding of reasoning capabilities in decoder-only transformer-based models. The code is available at: https://github.com/AnnonymousForPapers/CoT_Reasoning_Test.

papers.title: Cognitive Foundations for Reasoning and Their Manifestation in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do cognitive elements of reasoning manifest in LLMs, and how do they differ from human reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a taxonomy of 28 cognitive elements for reasoning and conducts a large-scale empirical analysis of human and LLM reasoning traces, revealing that LLMs underutilize cognitive elements correlated with success and that test-time reasoning guidance can improve performance.
papers.conclusion: The taxonomy provides a shared vocabulary for diagnosing reasoning failures and enables principled development of models that reason through robust cognitive mechanisms, while models possess latent capabilities that can be elicited with structural guidance.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs underutilize cognitive elements that are correlated with success, especially on ill-structured problems.
Humans use more abstraction and conceptual processing, while LLMs rely on surface-level enumeration.
Test-time reasoning guidance that scaffolds successful cognitive structures improves performance by up to 66.7% on complex problems.
The research community focuses on easily quantifiable cognitive elements (like sequential organization) and neglects meta-cognitive controls (like self-awareness).
Models possess behavioral repertoires associated with success but fail to deploy them spontaneously.
papers.limitation:
Human participants are educated adults; comparison with children might yield different insights.
Models are tested on a limited set of problem types.
future_direction: Using the taxonomy for training and evaluation of LLMs
Developing cognitive architectures based on the taxonomy
Extending the analysis to more problem types and models
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) solve complex problems yet fail on simpler variants, suggesting they achieve correct outputs through mechanisms fundamentally different from human reasoning. To understand this gap, we synthesize cognitive science research into a taxonomy of 28 cognitive elements spanning reasoning invariants, meta-cognitive controls, representations for organizing reasoning & knowledge, and transformation operations. We introduce a fine-grained evaluation framework and conduct the first large-scale empirical analysis of 192K traces from 18 models across text, vision, and audio, complemented by 54 human think-aloud traces, which we make publicly available. We find that models under-utilize cognitive elements correlated with success, narrowing to rigid sequential processing on ill-structured problems where diverse representations and meta-cognitive monitoring are critical. Human traces show more abstraction and conceptual processing, while models default to surface-level enumeration. Meta-analysis of 1.6K LLM reasoning papers reveals the research community concentrates on easily quantifiable elements (sequential organization: 55%, decomposition: 60%) but neglecting meta-cognitive controls (self-awareness: 16%) that correlate with success. Models possess behavioral repertoires associated with success but fail to deploy them spontaneously. Leveraging these patterns, we develop test-time reasoning guidance that automatically scaffold successful structures, improving performance by up to 66.7% on complex problems. By establishing a shared vocabulary between cognitive science and LLM research, our framework enables systematic diagnosis of reasoning failures and principled development of models that reason through robust cognitive mechanisms rather than spurious shortcuts, while providing tools to test theories of human cognition at scale.

papers.title: Deconstructing Attention: Investigating Design Principles for Effective Language Modeling
papers.research_question: Which design principles of dot-product attention are essential for effective language modeling, and can some be relaxed in hybrid architectures?
papers.core_contribution: Token mixing is indispensable for language modeling, while the mathematical form and sequence dependency can be relaxed, especially in hybrid architectures where standard attention layers stabilize simpler variants.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that token mixing is essential, but other attention principles can be simplified, especially when standard attention layers are interleaved, leading to robust performance.
papers.key_findings:
Token mixing is crucial; without it, models perform near-random on NLU tasks.
The standard mathematical form is important in uniform configurations but can be relaxed in hybrid ones.
Sequence-dependency enhances generalization ability.
Current QK derivation is not as essential as expected.
Layer collaboration allows poor-performing variants to contribute in hybrid architectures.
papers.limitation: Experiments are limited to models up to 500M parameters, 15B tokens pretraining, and monolingual tokenizer.
future_direction: Experimenting with larger models and different model families.
papers.abstract: The success of Transformer language models is widely credited to their dot-product attention mechanism, which interweaves a set of key design principles: mixing information across positions (enabling multi-token interactions), sequence-dependent activations (where attention weights adapt to each input), a specific mathematical form (dot-product similarities plus softmax weighting), and coupling of queries and keys to evolving hidden states (grounding attention in the current layer). However, the necessity of each of these principles remains largely untested. In this work, we systematically deconstruct attention by designing controlled variants that selectively relax these principles, applied both uniformly across all layers and in hybrid architectures where only some layers retain standard attention. Our empirical analysis reveals that mechanisms for mixing tokens are indispensable, as their absence collapses models to near-random behavior, while the exact mathematical form and sequence dependency can be substantially relaxed, especially when preserved in just a subset of layers. Surprisingly, even variants that fail in isolation can achieve robust performance when interleaved with standard attention, highlighting a cooperative effect. These findings deepen our understanding of what truly underpins attention's effectiveness and open new avenues for simplifying language models without sacrificing performance.

papers.title: How Chain-of-Thought Works? Tracing Information Flow from Decoding, Projection, and Activation
papers.research_question: How does Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting alter a model's internal states to improve reasoning performance?
papers.core_contribution: CoT works by constraining the decoding space via answer templates, with structural adherence strongly correlating with performance, and modulates neuron activation in a task-dependent manner (reducing activation in open-domain tasks, increasing it in closed-domain tasks).
papers.conclusion: The findings provide a novel mechanistic interpretability framework and critical insights for designing more efficient and robust CoT prompts.
papers.key_findings:
CoT prompts models to imitate structural keywords (e.g., 'time', 'action') from the prompt and content keywords (e.g., numbers) from the input question.
There is a strong positive correlation between adherence to the CoT reasoning structure (measured by Imitation Count) and task performance (accuracy).
CoT leads to more concentrated probability distributions (lower entropy) and higher confidence in generated tokens compared to standard prompting.
CoT reduces the average number of activated neurons in Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs) for open-domain tasks, but increases it for closed-domain tasks, indicating task-dependent modulation of neural engagement.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting significantly enhances model reasoning, yet its internal mechanisms remain poorly understood. We analyze CoT's operational principles by reversely tracing information flow across decoding, projection, and activation phases. Our quantitative analysis suggests that CoT may serve as a decoding space pruner, leveraging answer templates to guide output generation, with higher template adherence strongly correlating with improved performance. Furthermore, we surprisingly find that CoT modulates neuron engagement in a task-dependent manner: reducing neuron activation in open-domain tasks, yet increasing it in closed-domain scenarios. These findings offer a novel mechanistic interpretability framework and critical insights for enabling targeted CoT interventions to design more efficient and robust prompts. We released our code and data at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/cot-D247.

papers.title: Understanding Reasoning in Chain-of-Thought from the Hopfieldian View
papers.research_question: How does the reasoning capability emerge through Chain-of-Thought prompting? The paper aims to explain the fundamental factors behind CoT's success.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a Hopfieldian view of Chain-of-Thought reasoning, connecting it to cognitive neuroscience, and proposes the Representation-of-Thought framework to enhance robustness and interpretability of CoT reasoning.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a Hopfieldian framework for CoT interpretability, introducing error localization and the RoT framework, which improves robustness and interpretability of CoT reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
The Hopfieldian view provides a framework to understand CoT reasoning as movement between representation spaces.
A method for localizing reasoning errors in CoT responses is developed based on low-dimensional representation spaces.
The Representation-of-Thought (RoT) framework enhances the robustness of CoT reasoning by manipulating hidden states towards representation spaces.
Experimental results show RoT improves accuracy on arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning tasks.
RoT offers fine-grained control over the reasoning process and improves interpretability.
future_direction: Exploring other elements of the Hopfieldian view such as attractors and state space.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models have demonstrated remarkable abilities across various tasks, with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting emerging as a key technique to enhance reasoning capabilities. However, existing research primarily focuses on improving performance, lacking a comprehensive framework to explain and understand the fundamental factors behind CoT's success. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel perspective grounded in the Hopfieldian view of cognition in cognitive neuroscience. We establish a connection between CoT reasoning and key cognitive elements such as stimuli, actions, neural populations, and representation spaces. From our view, we can understand the reasoning process as the movement between these representation spaces. Building on this insight, we develop a method for localizing reasoning errors in the response of CoTs. Moreover, we propose the Representation-of-Thought (RoT) framework, which leverages the robustness of low-dimensional representation spaces to enhance the robustness of the reasoning process in CoTs. Experimental results demonstrate that RoT improves the robustness and interpretability of CoT reasoning while offering fine-grained control over the reasoning process.

papers.title: Circuit Stability Characterizes Language Model Generalization
papers.research_question: Can circuit stability characterize and predict generalization in language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces circuit stability as a method to assess model performance and shows it can characterize and predict different aspects of generalization.
papers.conclusion: Circuit stability characterizes generalization in language models and provides an actionable way to assess and improve model performance.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit stability predicts length, structural, and compositional generalization in arithmetic reasoning tasks.
Circuit instability in arithmetic indicates lack of understanding of commutativity and associativity.
For Boolean expression evaluation, circuit non-equivalence indicates structural generalization issues.
Chain-of-thought prompting induces circuit stability and improves performance.
Circuit stability is a robust estimator of model performance that can be computed efficiently.
papers.limitation:
Empirical case studies are limited in terms of tasks and models.
Computational cost of circuit discovery can be high for very large models.
Constructing partitions manually requires prior knowledge of the task.
future_direction: Extending circuit stability to other modalities and architectures.
Investigating the connection between circuit stability and generalization bounds.
Automating the construction of partitions for complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Extensively evaluating the capabilities of (large) language models is difficult. Rapid development of state-of-the-art models induce benchmark saturation, while creating more challenging datasets is labor-intensive. Inspired by the recent developments in mechanistic interpretability, we introduce circuit stability as a new way to assess model performance. Circuit stability refers to a model's ability to apply a consistent reasoning process-its circuit-across various inputs. We mathematically formalize circuit stability and circuit equivalence. Then, through three case studies, we empirically show that circuit stability and the lack thereof can characterize and predict different aspects of generalization. Our proposed methods offer a step towards rigorously relating the generality of models to their interpretability.

papers.title: Think-at-Hard: Selective Latent Iterations to Improve Reasoning Language Models
papers.research_question: Can LLMs selectively dedicate latent iterations only to hard tokens to improve reasoning capabilities under parameter constraints, avoiding latent overthinking?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Think-at-Hard (TaH), a dynamic latent thinking method that selectively applies deeper iterations only to hard tokens, using duo-causal attention, depth-specific LoRA adapters, and a neural iteration decider, with a stable two-stage training scheme.
papers.conclusion: TaH establishes a new paradigm for improving reasoning within current parameter budgets by selectively iterating deeper only on hard tokens, achieving consistent gains with minimal overhead.
papers.key_findings:
TaH improves reasoning accuracy across five challenging math benchmarks by 4.0-5.4% over strong single-iteration baselines with minimal overhead (<3% extra parameters, ≈6% extra iterations).
Fixed-depth recurrent transformers suffer from latent overthinking, where easy tokens are incorrectly revised in additional iterations, harming performance.
An oracle policy that iterates only on incorrectly predicted tokens (hard tokens) shows substantial performance gains, validating the selective iteration approach.
The duo-causal attention mechanism enables cross-depth information flow while maintaining full sequential parallelism during training and inference.
The two-stage training scheme (first backbone with oracle policy, then decider imitation) stabilizes the training of the tightly coupled LLM backbone and iteration decider.
papers.limitation: Performance comparisons with official Qwen3 models are not direct because the official models use different training data distributions, scales, and procedures (including on-policy distillation), while TaH uses only SFT on limited public data.
future_direction: Integrating TaH with online distillation to provide stronger supervision.
Applying reinforcement learning to optimize the compute–accuracy trade-off and learn continuation policies beyond imitation.
papers.abstract: Improving reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs), especially under parameter constraints, is crucial for real-world applications. Prior work proposes recurrent transformers, which allocate a fixed number of extra iterations per token to improve generation quality. After the first, standard forward pass, instead of verbalization, last-layer hidden states are fed back as inputs for additional iterations to refine token predictions. Yet we identify a latent overthinking phenomenon: easy token predictions that are already correct after the first pass are sometimes revised into errors in additional iterations. To address this, we propose Think-at-Hard (TaH), a dynamic latent thinking method that iterates deeper only at hard tokens. It employs a lightweight neural decider to trigger latent iterations only at tokens that are likely incorrect after the standard forward pass. During latent iterations, Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) modules shift the LLM objective from general next-token prediction to focused hard-token refinement. We further introduce a duo-causal attention mechanism that extends attention from the token sequence dimension to an additional iteration depth dimension. This enables cross-iteration information flow while maintaining full sequential parallelism. Experiments show that TaH boosts LLM reasoning performance across five challenging benchmarks while maintaining the same parameter count. Compared with baselines that iterate twice for all output tokens, TaH delivers 8.1-11.3% accuracy gains while exempting 94% of tokens from the second iteration. Against strong single-iteration Qwen3 models finetuned with the same data, it also delivers 4.0-5.0% accuracy gains. When allowing less than 3% additional parameters from LoRA and the iteration decider, the gains increase to 8.5-12.6% and 5.3-5.4%, respectively. Our code is available at https://github.com/thu-nics/TaH.

papers.title: Taming Knowledge Conflicts in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do language models handle knowledge conflicts between parametric memory and contextual information, and can we design a method to steer them towards either source without fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers the superposition of contextual information and parametric memory in attention heads and proposes JUICE, a test-time attention intervention method that steers LMs toward either parametric or contextual knowledge without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: JUICE sets a new state-of-the-art for handling knowledge conflicts, offering robust generalization across domains and conflict types, and is supported by theoretical analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads exhibit inconsistent behaviors under different degrees of knowledge conflict, challenging the notion of exclusive 'memory heads' and 'context heads'.
Combining individually effective interventions can lead to counteracting effects due to superposition.
JUICE achieves state-of-the-art performance in steering LMs towards parametric or contextual knowledge across diverse datasets and models.
JUICE is effective even with a very small head identification set (e.g., 4 samples).
The dual-run design of JUICE mitigates superposition effects and outperforms single-run interventions.
papers.abstract: Language Models (LMs) often encounter knowledge conflicts when parametric memory contradicts contextual knowledge. Previous works attribute this conflict to the interplay between "memory heads" and "context heads", attention heads assumed to promote either memory or context exclusively. In this study, we go beyond this fundamental assumption by uncovering a critical phenomenon we term the superposition of contextual information and parametric memory, where highly influential attention heads simultaneously contribute to both memory and context. Building upon this insight, we propose Just Run Twice (JuICE), a test-time attention intervention method that steers LMs toward either parametric beliefs or contextual knowledge without requiring fine-tuning. JuICE identifies a set of reliable attention heads and leverages a dual-run approach to mitigate the superposition effects. Extensive experiments across 11 datasets and 6 model architectures demonstrate that JuICE sets the new state-of-the-art performance and robust generalization, achieving significant and consistent improvement across different domains under various conflict types. Finally, we theoretically analyze knowledge conflict and the superposition of contextual information and parametric memory in attention heads, which further elucidates the effectiveness of JuICE in these settings. Our code is available at https://github.com/GaotangLi/JUICE.

papers.title: Understanding Hidden Computations in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do transformer models internally process and represent reasoning steps when Chain-of-Thought is replaced with filler characters, and can these hidden characters be recovered?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that hidden characters in filler Chain-of-Thought sequences can be recovered by analyzing layer-wise representations and token rankings without loss of performance, providing insights into internal mechanisms of transformer models.
papers.conclusion: The analysis sheds light on how models internally process and represent reasoning steps when explicit chain of thought is obscured, contributing to model interpretability and opening avenues for improving transparency in language model reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Layer-wise analysis reveals that filler tokens emerge in later layers, overwriting earlier numerical representations.
Token ranking analysis shows that original reasoning tokens remain among lower-ranked candidates beneath filler tokens.
A modified decoding algorithm can recover hidden characters by selecting non-filler tokens when fillers are top-ranked, without compromising task performance.
The model performs necessary computations in earlier layers and then overwrites intermediate representations with filler tokens in later layers to match training targets.
The findings suggest that models retain hidden reasoning steps internally even when outputting filler tokens.
papers.limitation: Focuses on a synthetic task (3SUM) and a relatively small transformer model, which may not capture complexities of real-world language tasks and larger models.
future_direction: Explore whether specific circuits, such as induction heads or particular attention patterns, are involved in overwriting behavior.
Apply similar analysis techniques to other tasks and models to assess the generality of the findings.
Extend the investigation to natural language tasks and larger models to determine if observed phenomena persist in more complex settings.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has significantly enhanced the reasoning abilities of large language models. However, recent studies have shown that models can still perform complex reasoning tasks even when the CoT is replaced with filler(hidden) characters (e.g., "..."), leaving open questions about how models internally process and represent reasoning steps. In this paper, we investigate methods to decode these hidden characters in transformer models trained with filler CoT sequences. By analyzing layer-wise representations using the logit lens method and examining token rankings, we demonstrate that the hidden characters can be recovered without loss of performance. Our findings provide insights into the internal mechanisms of transformer models and open avenues for improving interpretability and transparency in language model reasoning.

papers.title: Schoenfeld's Anatomy of Mathematical Reasoning by Language Models
papers.research_question: Do reasoning traces exhibit consistent structure when abstracted into functional episodes? How do reasoning dynamics differ across models? How do episode patterns correlate with correctness and efficiency?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ThinkARM, a framework for abstracting reasoning traces into functional episodes, enabling systematic analysis of reasoning structure and dynamics in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: Episode-level representations make reasoning steps explicit, enabling systematic analysis of how reasoning is structured, stabilized, and altered in modern language models.
papers.key_findings:
Episode-level analysis reveals a functional progression from abstract reasoning to concrete execution to evaluative control.
Reasoning models distribute effort across analysis, exploration, execution, and verification, while non-reasoning models are heavily execution-focused.
Exploration serves as a critical branching point: correct solutions route exploration into monitoring or re-analysis, while incorrect ones tend to continue execution or terminate.
Efficient reasoning methods selectively suppress evaluation-oriented episodes and feedback loops, diverging from base model patterns.
papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly expose reasoning traces, yet their underlying cognitive structure and steps remain difficult to identify and analyze beyond surface-level statistics. We adopt Schoenfeld's Episode Theory as an inductive, intermediate-scale lens and introduce ThinkARM (Anatomy of Reasoning in Models), a scalable framework that explicitly abstracts reasoning traces into functional reasoning steps such as Analysis, Explore, Implement, Verify, etc. When applied to mathematical problem solving by diverse models, this abstraction reveals reproducible thinking dynamics and structural differences between reasoning and non-reasoning models, which are not apparent from token-level views. We further present two diagnostic case studies showing that exploration functions as a critical branching step associated with correctness, and that efficiency-oriented methods selectively suppress evaluative feedback steps rather than uniformly shortening responses. Together, our results demonstrate that episode-level representations make reasoning steps explicit, enabling systematic analysis of how reasoning is structured, stabilized, and altered in modern language models.

papers.title: The Reasoning Trap: How Enhancing LLM Reasoning Amplifies Tool Hallucination
papers.abstract: Enhancing the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) is a key strategy for building Agents that "think then act." However, recent observations, like OpenAI's o3, suggest a paradox: stronger reasoning often coincides with increased hallucination, yet no prior work has systematically examined whether reasoning enhancement itself causes tool hallucination. To address this gap, we pose the central question: Does strengthening reasoning increase tool hallucination? To answer this, we introduce SimpleToolHalluBench, a diagnostic benchmark measuring tool hallucination in two failure modes: (i) no tool available, and (ii) only distractor tools available. Through controlled experiments, we establish three key findings. First, we demonstrate a causal relationship: progressively enhancing reasoning through RL increases tool hallucination proportionally with task performance gains. Second, this effect transcends overfitting - training on non-tool tasks (e.g., mathematics) still amplifies subsequent tool hallucination. Third, the effect is method-agnostic, appearing when reasoning is instilled via supervised fine-tuning and when it is merely elicited at inference by switching from direct answers to step-by-step thinking. We also evaluate mitigation strategies including Prompt Engineering and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), revealing a fundamental reliability-capability trade-off: reducing hallucination consistently degrades utility. Mechanistically, Reasoning RL disproportionately collapses tool-reliability-related representations, and hallucinations surface as amplified divergences concentrated in late-layer residual streams. These findings reveal that current reasoning enhancement methods inherently amplify tool hallucination, highlighting the need for new training objectives that jointly optimize for capability and reliability.

papers.title: Finding Highly Interpretable Prompt-Specific Circuits in Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether circuits in language models are prompt-specific rather than task-level, and introduces a method to identify and analyze these prompt-specific circuits.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that circuits in language models are prompt-specific rather than task-level, and introduces ACC++, a method to identify and analyze these prompt-specific circuits, revealing that prompts form families with representative circuits.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that circuits should be analyzed at the prompt level, and ACC++ enables scalable interpretability by identifying prompt-specific circuit families.
papers.key_findings:
ACC++ provides cleaner, lower-dimensional causal signals compared to ACC.
Circuits in language models are prompt-specific, with no single circuit per task.
Prompts form clusters into families with similar circuits, allowing for representative circuits.
Signal analysis reveals stable routes and functional redundancy across prompt families.
An automated pipeline can generate interpretable explanations for circuit signals.
papers.abstract: Understanding the internal circuits that language models use to solve tasks remains a central challenge in mechanistic interpretability. Most prior work identifies circuits at the task level by averaging across many prompts, implicitly assuming a single stable mechanism per task. We show that this assumption can obscure a crucial source of structure: circuits are prompt-specific, even within a fixed task. Building on attention causal communication (ACC) (Franco & Crovella, 2025), we introduce ACC++, refinements that extract cleaner, lower-dimensional causal signals inside attention heads from a single forward pass. Like ACC, our approach does not require replacement models (e.g., SAEs) or activation patching; ACC++ further improves circuit precision by reducing attribution noise. Applying ACC++ to indirect object identification (IOI) in GPT-2, Pythia, and Gemma 2, we find there is no single circuit for IOI in any model: different prompt templates induce systematically different mechanisms. Despite this variation, prompts cluster into prompt families with similar circuits, and we propose a representative circuit for each family as a practical unit of analysis. Finally, we develop an automated interpretability pipeline that uses ACC++ signals to surface human-interpretable features and assemble mechanistic explanations for prompt families behavior. Together, our results recast circuits as a meaningful object of study by shifting the unit of analysis from tasks to prompts, enabling scalable circuit descriptions in the presence of prompt-specific mechanisms.

papers.title: The Illusion of Thinking
papers.research_question: What are the fundamental capabilities, scaling properties, and limitations of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) that generate detailed thinking processes?
papers.core_contribution: This paper systematically investigates the reasoning capabilities of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) using controllable puzzle environments, revealing three performance regimes based on problem complexity and a fundamental scaling limit where reasoning effort decreases beyond a critical complexity threshold despite adequate token budget.
papers.conclusion: Current Large Reasoning Models demonstrate improved performance on medium-complexity tasks but exhibit fundamental scaling limitations and complete collapse at high complexities, raising questions about their true reasoning capabilities and the need for more robust reasoning approaches.
papers.key_findings:
Frontier LRMs face a complete accuracy collapse beyond certain problem complexities across different puzzle environments.
There exist three distinct performance regimes: low-complexity tasks where standard LLMs outperform LRMs, medium-complexity tasks where LRMs show an advantage, and high-complexity tasks where both models collapse.
LRMs exhibit a counterintuitive scaling limit: reasoning effort (thinking tokens) increases with problem complexity up to a point, then declines despite having an adequate token budget.
Analysis of reasoning traces shows that in simpler problems, LRMs often identify correct solutions early but inefficiently continue exploring (overthinking), while at moderate complexity correct solutions emerge only after extensive exploration of incorrect paths.
LRMs have limitations in exact computation, failing to use explicit algorithms and reasoning inconsistently across puzzle types.
papers.limitation: The study focuses on specific puzzle environments which, while controllable, may not fully capture the breadth of real-world reasoning tasks.
papers.abstract: Recent generations of frontier language models have introduced Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) that generate detailed thinking processes before providing answers. While these models demonstrate improved performance on reasoning benchmarks, their fundamental capabilities, scaling properties, and limitations remain insufficiently understood. Current evaluations primarily focus on established mathematical and coding benchmarks, emphasizing final answer accuracy. However, this evaluation paradigm often suffers from data contamination and does not provide insights into the reasoning traces’ structure and quality. In this work, we systematically investigate these gaps with the help of controllable puzzle environments that allow precise manipulation of compositional complexity while maintaining consistent logical structures. This setup enables the analysis of not only final answers but also the internal reasoning traces, offering insights into how LRMs “think”. Through extensive experimentation across diverse puzzles, we show that frontier LRMs face a complete accuracy collapse beyond certain complexities. Moreover, they exhibit a counterintuitive scaling limit: their reasoning effort increases with problem complexity up to a point, then declines despite having an adequate token budget. By comparing LRMs with their standard LLM counterparts under equivalent inference compute, we identify three performance regimes: (1) lowcomplexity tasks where standard models surprisingly outperform LRMs, (2) medium-complexity tasks where additional thinking in LRMs demonstrates advantage, and (3) high-complexity tasks where both models experience complete collapse. We found that LRMs have limitations in exact computation: they fail to use explicit algorithms and reason inconsistently across puzzles. We also investigate the reasoning traces in more depth, studying the patterns of explored solutions and analyzing the models’ computational behavior, shedding light on their strengths, limitations, and ultimately raising crucial questions about their true reasoning capabilities.

papers.title: Adaptive Circuit Behavior and Generalization in Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How well does the indirect object identification (IOI) circuit in GPT-2 small generalize to prompt variants that challenge the assumptions of its algorithm?
papers.core_contribution: The IOI circuit generalizes surprisingly well to prompt variants, reusing all its components and mechanisms while only adding additional input edges, and a mechanism called S2 Hacking explains how the circuit outperforms the full model on these variants.
papers.conclusion: The IOI circuit in GPT-2 small generalizes more effectively than previously understood, reusing its core components and mechanisms while adapting through minimal structural changes, offering insights into the broader capabilities of large neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
The base IOI circuit outperforms the full model on DoubleIO and TripleIO prompt variants where the IOI algorithm would fail.
A mechanism termed S2 Hacking explains how the circuit achieves high performance on these variants by focusing on the S2 token due to the knockout procedure.
New circuits discovered for DoubleIO and TripleIO variants reuse all components of the base IOI circuit, only adding edges from additional input tokens (IO2 for DoubleIO, IO2 and IO3 for TripleIO).
The circuit components (attention heads) largely retain their functionalities from the base IOI task when evaluated on the variants.
The order of names in the prompt affects performance, with a 'first come, first serve' mechanism observed in a Previous Token head (2.2).
future_direction: a more detailed study of the duplicate suppression mechanism
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand the inner workings of large neural networks by identifying circuits, or minimal subgraphs within the model that implement algorithms responsible for performing specific tasks. These circuits are typically discovered and analyzed using a narrowly defined prompt format. However, given the abilities of large language models (LLMs) to generalize across various prompt formats for the same task, it remains unclear how well these circuits generalize. For instance, it is unclear whether the models generalization results from reusing the same circuit components, the components behaving differently, or the use of entirely different components. In this paper, we investigate the generality of the indirect object identification (IOI) circuit in GPT-2 small, which is well-studied and believed to implement a simple, interpretable algorithm. We evaluate its performance on prompt variants that challenge the assumptions of this algorithm. Our findings reveal that the circuit generalizes surprisingly well, reusing all of its components and mechanisms while only adding additional input edges. Notably, the circuit generalizes even to prompt variants where the original algorithm should fail; we discover a mechanism that explains this which we term S2 Hacking. Our findings indicate that circuits within LLMs may be more flexible and general than previously recognized, underscoring the importance of studying circuit generalization to better understand the broader capabilities of these models.

papers.title: Attention over learned object embeddings enables complex visual\n reasoning
papers.research_question: Can a neural-network-based approach combining learned object-centric representations, self-attention, and self-supervised dynamics learning achieve state-of-the-art performance on complex visual reasoning tasks without task-specific modular components?
papers.core_contribution: The Aloe model, which combines learned object-centric representations, self-attention, and self-supervised dynamics learning, achieves state-of-the-art performance on three visual reasoning tasks without task-specific modular components, demonstrating that flexibility and performance need not be traded off.
papers.conclusion: The success of Aloe suggests that with the right soft biases and learning objectives—object-centric representations, self-attention, and self-supervised dynamics learning—neural networks can achieve strong performance on spatiotemporal reasoning tasks without resorting to task-specific modular components.
papers.key_findings:
Aloe outperforms previous state-of-the-art models on CLEVRER, CATER, and ACRE across various question and reasoning types.
The combination of object-level discretization, global self-attention, and self-supervised learning is crucial for strong performance; ablations of any component lead to significant drops.
Aloe is data-efficient, matching previous SOTA performance on CLEVRER with only 50-60% of the training data.
The model generalizes across three distinct visual reasoning tasks (CLEVRER, CATER, ACRE) without any architectural modifications.
Qualitative analysis of attention weights shows the model aligns objects across time and focuses on relevant objects and words for answering questions.
papers.limitation:
Applied only to synthetic datasets due to a lack of real-world datasets testing higher-order spatiotemporal reasoning.
The domains used may not fully evaluate the intended capacities due to hidden biases or other factors.
May perpetuate biases found in training data and could invite problematic applications involving automated assignment of blame.
future_direction: Applying the approach to real-world datasets, such as the upcoming Traffic QA.
Investigating other self-supervised losses and masking schemes to further improve dynamics learning.
Designing and developing more challenging tasks that better approximate human-level visual, spatiotemporal, and causal reasoning.
papers.abstract:
Neural networks have achieved success in a wide array of perceptual tasks but
often fail at tasks involving both perception and higher-level reasoning. On
these more challenging tasks, bespoke approaches (such as modular symbolic
components, independent dynamics models or semantic parsers) targeted towards
that specific type of task have typically performed better. The downside to
these targeted approaches, however, is that they can be more brittle than
general-purpose neural networks, requiring significant modification or even
redesign according to the particular task at hand. Here, we propose a more
general neural-network-based approach to dynamic visual reasoning problems that
obtains state-of-the-art performance on three different domains, in each case
outperforming bespoke modular approaches tailored specifically to the task. Our
method relies on learned object-centric representations, self-attention and
self-supervised dynamics learning, and all three elements together are required
for strong performance to emerge. The success of this combination suggests that
there may be no need to trade off flexibility for performance on problems
involving spatio-temporal or causal-style reasoning. With the right soft biases
and learning objectives in a neural network we may be able to attain the best
of both worlds.

papers.title: Attention Interpretability Across NLP Tasks
papers.research_question: This paper investigates the interpretability of attention weights in neural network models, specifically addressing when attention weights are interpretable and when they are not.
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a comprehensive explanation for when attention weights are interpretable, showing that attention is interpretable when it is essential for the model's prediction and cannot be reduced to a gating unit, and validates this through experiments on diverse NLP tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that attention weights are interpretable and correlated with feature importance measures when they are essential for the model's prediction and cannot be reduced to a gating unit.
papers.key_findings:
Attention weights in single sequence tasks (like text classification) can be interpreted as a gating unit and are not interpretable as explanations.
For pair sequence and generation tasks, attention weights are crucial and interpretable.
Altering attention weights in single sequence tasks does not substantially affect performance, while in pair sequence and generation tasks it does.
Attention weights in single sequence tasks do not correlate well with feature importance measures, but they do in pair sequence and generation tasks.
Manual evaluation shows that attention weights in single sequence tasks do not provide a reason for the prediction, while in pair sequence tasks they do.
papers.abstract: The attention layer in a neural network model provides insights into the model's reasoning behind its prediction, which are usually criticized for being opaque. Recently, seemingly contradictory viewpoints have emerged about the interpretability of attention weights (Jain & Wallace, 2019; Vig & Belinkov, 2019). Amid such confusion arises the need to understand attention mechanism more systematically. In this work, we attempt to fill this gap by giving a comprehensive explanation which justifies both kinds of observations (i.e., when is attention interpretable and when it is not). Through a series of experiments on diverse NLP tasks, we validate our observations and reinforce our claim of interpretability of attention through manual evaluation.

papers.title: Lost at the Beginning of Reasoning
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) have significantly advanced complex reasoning capabilities, particularly through extended chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning that incorporates mechanisms such as backtracking, self-reflection, and self-correction. Despite these developments, the self-correction abilities of LLMs during long CoT reasoning remain underexplored. And recent findings on overthinking suggest that such models often engage in unnecessarily redundant reasoning. In this work, we empirically show that the first reasoning step exerts a disproportionately large influence on the final prediction. I.e., errors introduced at this stage can substantially degrade subsequent reasoning quality. This phenomenon is consistently observed across various state-of-the-art open- and closed-source reasoning models. Leveraging this insight, we propose an efficient sampling strategy that leverages a reward model to identify and retain high-quality first reasoning steps while discarding suboptimal ones, achieving up to a 70% reduction in inference cost without sacrificing any accuracy. Our work highlights the central role of the first reasoning step in generating a high-quality reasoning trajectory, and thus enabling significantly efficient sampling.

papers.title: Large Language Models Are Human-Like Internally
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether surprisal (negative log probability) from internal layers of large language models aligns with human sentence processing data, and whether the alignment varies by layer depth and the type of human measure (behavioral vs. neurophysiological).
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that surprisal from internal layers of larger language models aligns well with human sentence processing data, challenging prior conclusions that focused on final layers. Additionally, it finds that earlier layers align with fast human measures (e.g., gaze duration) and later layers with slower measures (e.g., N400).
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that larger language models are cognitively plausible when internal layers are considered, and that different layers correspond to different stages of human sentence processing, advocating for layer-wise alignment in cognitive modeling.
papers.key_findings:
Surprisal from internal layers of larger LMs aligns with human sentence processing data as well as or better than smaller LMs.
The last layer does not yield the best alignment; the best layer varies by human measure.
Earlier layers align better with fast human measures (e.g., first-pass gaze duration, self-paced reading time), while later layers align better with slower measures (e.g., N400, MAZE processing time).
When considering the best internal layer, larger LMs show a positive scaling effect (larger models have higher ∆LL) for most human measures.
The alignment patterns are consistent across multiple languages (tested on MECO corpus).
papers.limitation: The study is focused on naturalistic reading corpora and does not include controlled experiments on syntactic ambiguity or grammatical violation, which are known challenges for surprisal theory.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to other probability-based measures such as entropy and entropy reduction.
Combine the internal layer approach with linguistically-motivated neural models.
papers.abstract: Recent cognitive modeling studies have reported that larger language models (LMs) exhibit a poorer fit to human reading behavior (Oh and Schuler, 2023b; Shain et al., 2024; Kuribayashi et al., 2024), leading to claims of their cognitive implausibility. In this paper, we revisit this argument through the lens of mechanistic interpretability and argue that prior conclusions were skewed by an exclusive focus on the final layers of LMs. Our analysis reveals that next-word probabilities derived from internal layers of larger LMs align with human sentence processing data as well as, or better than, those from smaller LMs. This alignment holds consistently across behavioral (self-paced reading times, gaze durations, MAZE task processing times) and neurophysiological (N400 brain potentials) measures, challenging earlier mixed results and suggesting that the cognitive plausibility of larger LMs has been underestimated. Furthermore, we first identify an intriguing relationship between LM layers and human measures: earlier layers correspond more closely with fast gaze durations, while later layers better align with relatively slower signals such as N400 potentials and MAZE processing times. Our work opens new avenues for interdisciplinary research at the intersection of mechanistic interpretability and cognitive modeling.

papers.title: Is Random Attention Sufficient for Sequence Modeling? Disentangling Trainable Components in the Transformer
papers.research_question: How much, and which aspects, of transformer performance gains can be attributed to the self-attention mechanism, and which degrees of freedom inside the Transformer are truly necessary for its behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that transformers with frozen query and key weights (Frozen-QK) can still form induction heads and perform competitively on language modeling, and that a transformer with entirely random, static attention (MixiT) can perform well on tasks that do not require in-context reasoning, highlighting the distinct roles of attention and MLPs.
papers.conclusion: The transformer architecture has a built-in inductive bias towards forming specialized circuits, and different components (attention and MLPs) are responsible for different capabilities, with attention largely responsible for in-context reasoning and MLPs for memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Frozen-QK, with random attention weights, can form induction heads and achieve competitive language modeling performance.
MixiT, with entirely random static attention, solves algorithmic tasks but fails at tasks requiring in-context reasoning like retrieval.
MLPs are crucial for memorization and collaborate with attention for knowledge storage.
The transformer architecture has an inductive bias towards forming specialized circuits even without learnable attention weights.
MixiT overcomes depth-wise scaling challenges of prior random transformers via stable signal propagation.
papers.limitation: MixiT cannot form input-dependent specialized circuits like induction heads, limiting its performance on tasks requiring in-context reasoning.
future_direction: Further study on why increasing the number of attention heads does not improve performance for some tasks, such as Yelp sentiment classification.
papers.abstract: The transformer architecture is central to the success of modern Large Language Models (LLMs), in part due to its surprising ability to perform a wide range of tasks - including mathematical reasoning, memorization, and retrieval - using only gradient-based learning on next-token prediction. While the core component of a transformer is the self-attention mechanism, we question how much, and which aspects, of the performance gains can be attributed to it. To this end, we compare standard transformers to variants in which either the MLP layers or the attention weights are frozen at initialization. Surprisingly, we find that attention with frozen key and query weights is not only able to form induction heads, but can also perform competitively on language modeling. We formalize this by proving a new expressivity result for transformer models with frozen key and query weights. To further isolate the contribution of attention, we design MixiT, an architecture with entirely random attention scores, with provably stable signal propagation that overcomes prior depth-wise scaling challenges in random transformers. We use the successes and failures of MixiT to understand the role each transformer component plays, such as attention being largely responsible for in-context reasoning, and MLPs being responsible for, but collaborates with attention, on knowledge storage. Our results suggest that the transformer architecture has a built-in inductive bias towards forming specialized circuits, as it does even without learnable attention weights.

papers.title: Scaling sparse feature circuit finding for in-context learning
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be used to understand the mechanism of in-context learning in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that sparse autoencoders can identify task-detection and task-execution features in the in-context learning circuit of large language models, and introduces the Task Vector Cleaning algorithm to decompose task vectors into interpretable features.
papers.conclusion: The findings advance understanding of in-context learning mechanisms and demonstrate the potential of sparse autoencoders as a powerful tool for interpretability research on larger language models.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs can be used to analyze in-context learning in larger models like Gemma-1 2B, scaling up circuit analysis.
Task-execution features encode task knowledge and can causally induce task zero-shot performance.
Task-detection features identify tasks from the prompt and are causally linked to execution features via attention and MLP sublayers.
The Task Vector Cleaning algorithm effectively decomposes task vectors into sparse, interpretable features while preserving their effect on loss.
The in-context learning circuit involves interaction between detection and execution features through attention and MLP layers.
papers.limitation:
Circuit search was constrained to intermediate layers due to early layers processing token-level information and having lower quality Indirect Effect approximations.
Hundreds of features needed to be ablated to achieve significant faithfulness degradation, unlike prior work which required fewer.
Negative steering experiments showed lower task specificity, indicating steering experiments alone may not suffice for comprehensive analysis.
future_direction: Improving SAE training to yield more monosemantic features.
Scaling circuit analysis to even larger models.
Applying these techniques to more complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular tool for interpreting large language model activations, but their utility in addressing open questions in interpretability remains unclear. In this work, we demonstrate their effectiveness by using SAEs to deepen our understanding of the mechanism behind in-context learning (ICL). We identify abstract SAE features that (i) encode the model's knowledge of which task to execute and (ii) whose latent vectors causally induce the task zero-shot. This aligns with prior work showing that ICL is mediated by task vectors. We further demonstrate that these task vectors are well approximated by a sparse sum of SAE latents, including these task-execution features. To explore the ICL mechanism, we adapt the sparse feature circuits methodology of Marks et al. (2024) to work for the much larger Gemma-1 2B model, with 30 times as many parameters, and to the more complex task of ICL. Through circuit finding, we discover task-detecting features with corresponding SAE latents that activate earlier in the prompt, that detect when tasks have been performed. They are causally linked with task-execution features through the attention and MLP sublayers.

papers.title: Learning to Deceive with Attention-Based Explanations
papers.research_question: Do attention scores necessarily indicate features that influence a model's predictions? Can attention be manipulated to produce deceptive explanations while the model still relies on impermissible tokens?
papers.core_contribution: Attention mechanisms can be easily manipulated during training to produce deceptive explanations that assign low weight to impermissible tokens, while models continue to rely on those tokens for prediction, casting doubt on attention's reliability for auditing models.
papers.conclusion: Attention is easily manipulable with minimal accuracy cost, raising concerns about its use as a tool for model auditing and transparency.
papers.key_findings:
A simple training scheme can severely reduce attention mass on impermissible tokens with little to no decrease in task accuracy.
Human studies show that manipulated attention explanations deceive participants into thinking biased models do not rely on gender information.
Manipulated models cheat by passing information through recurrent connections or by increasing the magnitude of representations for impermissible tokens.
For sequence-to-sequence tasks, manipulated attention models outperform no-attention and uniform attention baselines, indicating attention adds value beyond alignment.
Different random seeds lead to different alternative mechanisms for maintaining performance while reducing attention on impermissible tokens.
papers.abstract: Attention mechanisms are ubiquitous components in neural architectures applied to natural language processing. In addition to yielding gains in predictive accuracy, attention weights are often claimed to confer interpretability, purportedly useful both for providing insights to practitioners and for explaining why a model makes its decisions to stakeholders. We call the latter use of attention mechanisms into question by demonstrating a simple method for training models to produce deceptive attention masks. Our method diminishes the total weight assigned to designated impermissible tokens, even when the models can be shown to nevertheless rely on these features to drive predictions. Across multiple models and tasks, our approach manipulates attention weights while paying surprisingly little cost in accuracy. Through a human study, we show that our manipulated attention-based explanations deceive people into thinking that predictions from a model biased against gender minorities do not rely on the gender. Consequently, our results cast doubt on attention's reliability as a tool for auditing algorithms in the context of fairness and accountability. 1

papers.title: CoT-Space: A Theoretical Framework for Internal Slow-Thinking via Reinforcement Learning
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether classical learning theories can be revitalized to understand LLM reasoning via reinforcement learning, by bridging the gap between token-level RL and reasoning-level Chain-of-Thought.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CoT-Space, a theoretical framework that recasts LLM reasoning from discrete token prediction to optimization in a continuous semantic space, bridging classical learning theory to explain phenomena like overthinking and providing a foundation for more principled reasoning agents.
papers.conclusion: The CoT-Space framework provides a theoretical foundation for understanding LLM reasoning via RL, revitalizing classical learning theories to guide the development of more effective and generalizable reasoning agents.
papers.key_findings:
The convergence to an optimal Chain-of-Thought length is a natural consequence of the trade-off between underfitting and overfitting.
The optimal CoT length increases with the intrinsic difficulty of the task.
The framework provides explanations for hallucination (trapped optimization), prompt sensitivity (landscape instability), emergent abilities (topological phase transition), and the efficacy of external slow-thinking strategies.
papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has become a pivotal approach for enhancing the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, a significant theoretical gap persists, as traditional token-level RL frameworks fail to align with the reasoning-level nature of complex, multi-step thought processes like Chain-of-Thought (CoT).
